disease_info: Bulimia nervosa is an eating disorder characterized by recurrent episodes of consuming unusually large amounts of food accompanied by a sense of loss of control, followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (such as vomiting, fasting, excessive exercise, or misuse of laxatives/diuretics) aimed at preventing weight gain. Self-evaluation is unduly influenced by body shape and weight, but individuals typically maintain a body weight within or near the normal range, distinguishing it from anorexia nervosa. The course is often chronic or relapsing, with symptoms waxing and waning in response to stress, interpersonal difficulties, and changes in life structure or mood. It must be differentiated from binge-eating disorder, which lacks regular compensatory behaviors, and from primary mood or anxiety disorders where eating changes are secondary rather than driven by weight/shape concerns.

narrative.personality: A methodical, solitary man who finds comfort in routines and quiet, hands-on hobbies, and occasionally uses small indulgences as a private form of rebellion against his otherwise tightly controlled life.
narrative.stressor: After his divorce three years ago, Stephen’s life narrowed to work, solitary evenings, and his garden, and he began to lean heavily on cooking large, rich meals as both a hobby and his main source of comfort. When his ex-wife started dating someone he perceived as fitter and more successful, casual comments from coworkers about him “slowing down” and putting on a bit of weight struck a nerve, activating long-standing insecurities about being replaceable and unremarkable. In response, he became increasingly rigid and self-punitive about his eating and exercise, oscillating between periods of private overeating during lonely evenings and extreme attempts to “make up for it” through restrictive routines and long walks, all while trying to maintain his meticulous image at work. Over six months, the cycle intensified to the point that his energy and concentration at the register began to falter and he withdrew from friends on the trails, leading him to seek help after his sister remarked that his relationship with food and exercise seemed to be “running his life instead of the other way around.”
narrative.chief_complaint: “I spend a lot of time trying to undo what I eat with strict dieting and exercise, and it’s getting out of hand.”

narrative.personality: A gentle, community‑minded retiree who balances practical handiwork with reflective, artistic pursuits and takes quiet pride in staying active and useful to others.
narrative.stressor: Following a minor cardiac scare and a stern warning from his doctor about his blood pressure and cholesterol, Daniel became preoccupied with the idea that gaining any weight would threaten his independence and ability to keep working in his garden and volunteering. He began reading diet advice online and in magazines, internalizing strict rules about “good” and “bad” foods that clashed with the communal meals and baked goods that were a big part of his social life at the senior center. When he did allow himself to eat more at family gatherings or potlucks, he would later respond with increasingly rigid attempts to compensate—skipping meals, walking or doing chores far beyond his usual routine, and quietly berating himself for perceived lapses. Over six months, this push‑pull between enjoying food in social settings and then trying to “fix” it afterward left him feeling ashamed and fatigued, and after a volunteer coordinator gently asked why he seemed so worn down and anxious about food at events, he agreed to talk with a mental health professional at the clinic attached to the senior center.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Whenever I eat more than I think I should, I feel like I have to overdo it with cutting back or extra activity afterward.”

narrative.personality: A highly organized, competitive senior developer who thrives on structure, measurable goals, and out‑performing peers both at work and in his numerous structured hobbies.
narrative.stressor: In the year after his divorce, Marvin threw himself into work and his bowling league, finding validation in performance metrics and rankings, and he gradually extended that same competitive mindset to his body as his company introduced wellness challenges and step‑count leaderboards. Surrounded by younger, leaner colleagues and bombarded with fitness app statistics and locker‑room banter about body fat percentages, he became fixated on the idea that maintaining a certain physique was essential to being taken seriously in the fast‑paced tech culture and to proving he hadn’t “let himself go” after the marriage ended. He began cycling through periods of strict food control followed by episodes of eating well beyond what he had planned during late‑night coding or debugging sessions, then reacting with increasingly extreme and secretive methods to try to control his weight, all while meticulously tracking every fluctuation on smart scales and apps. Over six months, this preoccupation with weight and shape came to dominate his self‑evaluation, contributing to sleep disruption, irritability with his team, and withdrawal from social events where food was involved, and he finally sought psychiatric help after realizing that his mood and daily decisions were being dictated almost entirely by how his body looked and what he had eaten that day.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My whole sense of how I’m doing depends on what the scale says and how my body looks, and it’s starting to take over everything.”
